text:
I want to write a request for promotion to senior paralegal. I've been a paralegal in the litigation group of a 60-lawyer law firm for 5 years.

Facts:
- I support 4 lawyers and worked on 23 cases last year, including 2 that went to trial.
- I built the group's tracking sheet for court deadlines in 2023. Two other groups in the firm now use it.
- Last March I entered a filing deadline wrong in that same sheet. Another paralegal noticed, and we filed 2 hours before the court's cutoff. After that I added a second-person check to the sheet.
- I billed 1,640 hours last year. The group's target is 1,550.
- I trained the 3 paralegals the group hired in the last 2 years.
- A senior paralegal is paid $9,000 a year more and supervises the other paralegals.

Keep it under 400 words. It goes to the managing partner of our group.

Before I draft, a few questions. Your answers will change what the request says:

1. **Is there an open senior paralegal role, or are you asking the firm to create one?** These are different requests. Asking to fill a vacancy is a fairly simple case. Asking for a new role means showing the group needs a supervisor now, and your training of the 3 new hires is the natural evidence for that.

2. **Since March, has the second-person check caught any other errors, and have there been any more deadline problems?** The managing partner probably knows about March. The letter will mention it plainly, next to what you did about it. Proof that the fix has worked would answer the obvious doubt.

3. **Do you already do supervisory work beyond the initial training?** For example, assigning work, reviewing the new paralegals' work, or being the person they come to with questions. Are those 3 paralegals still with the group and doing well? The senior role is mainly about supervising, so this is the evidence that matters most.

4. **Would any of your 4 lawyers back this request, or have your recent reviews said anything you can quote?** Someone the partner trusts vouching for your work makes a much stronger case than your own account.

5. **What exactly are you asking for, and by when?** For instance, a meeting to discuss it, a decision before annual reviews, or promotion from a specific date. Should the letter mention the $9,000 or leave pay for a later conversation?

6. **What names should I use?** The managing partner's name and how you address them (first name or formal), and your name for the signature. Also: does the partner know about anything else the letter leaves out, such as a weak spot or another candidate for the role? It's better to deal with it in the letter than to have it come up afterward.

If you don't know an answer, just say so. I'll write around it and won't guess.

1. I don't know if there's an open role.
2. Since the second-person check went in last April, there have been no wrong or missed deadlines in about 600 entries. I don't know if it's caught other errors.
3. I don't know beyond the training. Of the 3 I trained, one left after 8 months.
4. I don't know.
5. I'd like to meet with him in person to talk about it. Requests are due December 15 and promotions are decided in the January review cycle. On pay, go with what you recommend.
6. I'm Jenna Morales. The managing partner is David Kessler. I don't know first name vs formal. Weak spots: I can't promise I'll never make an error again. I can commit to running a short weekly check-in with the paralegals I'd supervise, and to finishing the state paralegal certification by next June.

I wrote this as an email you can send before the December 15 deadline. It's about 340 words.

<final_document>
**Subject:** Request for promotion to Senior Paralegal

Dear David,

I'd like to be considered for promotion to senior paralegal in the January review cycle. I'd also like to meet with you in person before then to talk about it.

I've been a paralegal in the litigation group for five years. Last year I supported four lawyers on 23 cases, two of which went to trial. I billed 1,640 hours against the group's target of 1,550.

I already do much of what the senior role involves. I trained all three paralegals the group has hired in the last two years. Two are still with us, and one left after eight months. If I'm promoted, I'll hold a short weekly check-in with the paralegals I supervise, so that their questions and problems come up early and not when a deadline is close.

In 2023 I built the group's tracking sheet for court deadlines. Two other groups in the firm now use it.

That sheet is also where I made my most serious mistake. Last March I entered a filing deadline wrong. Another paralegal noticed, and we filed two hours before the court's cutoff. I can't promise I'll never make another error. What I could do was make sure that one person's error doesn't reach a filing. In April I added a second-person check to the sheet. Since then there have been no wrong or missed deadlines in about 600 entries. I'd bring the same approach to supervising: build checks that catch mistakes instead of counting on nobody making one.

I will also complete the state paralegal certification by June 2027.

Could we meet at a time that suits you before the January review? I'd value the chance to hear what you'd need to see from me in the role.

Thank you for considering this.

Best regards,
Jenna Morales
</final_document>

Some decisions you may want to change:

- **Pay:** I left the $9,000 out. David knows what the role pays. Naming the figure would make the conversation about cost when it should be about whether you're ready for the job. If he raises pay in the meeting, you'll be ready for it.
- **The trainee who left:** I included it, stated once and followed by your weekly check-in commitment. David almost certainly knows about it, and mentioning it yourself makes your other numbers more believable. I didn't give a reason for the departure because you didn't give me one. If it had nothing to do with the training (for example, the person moved away), adding half a sentence would help.
- **Greeting:** I used "Dear David," which is normal for an internal email at most firms. If your group is more formal, change it to "Dear Mr. Kessler."
- **Worth finding out before the meeting:** whether there's an open senior role, and whether one of your four lawyers would speak up for you. Either would strengthen your case, and neither needs to be in the email.
